Aierth Technologies • 2025

Building a technology education brand designed around opportunity.

Aierth Technologies is a technology and digital education company built around a simple but ambitious idea:

Make access to relevant technology skills more practical, accessible, and connected to real career opportunities.

I worked across the brand and digital product experience, translating Aierth's business vision into a visual identity, website experience, marketing ecosystem, and scalable design language.

The goal wasn't simply to make Aierth look like another tech company.

It was to create a brand that could communicate technology, ambition, credibility, learning, and opportunity while still feeling approachable to the people it was built for.

  • Brand Identity
  • Product Design
  • UX/UI
  • Web Design
  • Design System
  • Marketing
  • Graphic Design
  • Social media management

The challenge

Aierth was growing from an idea into a technology education brand.

That meant the design needed to solve more than a visual identity problem.

The brand needed to communicate:

What Aierth does

Why it exists

Who it is for

Why someone should trust it

What makes its learning experience different

How education connects to career opportunities

At the same time, the digital experience needed to support multiple business goals:

Discover → Understand → Explore → Trust → Enroll

The challenge was therefore to create a system that could work across brand, website, courses, campaigns, social media, and future digital products without feeling fragmented.

The Opportunity

Aierth's bigger vision went beyond teaching individual courses.

The business was being shaped around a broader technology ecosystem

— one where people could develop practical skills and eventually connect those skills to professional opportunities.

That gave the design a much bigger responsibility.

I wasn't designing a website in isolation.

I was designing the first layer of an ecosystem.

Product Designer / Brand Designer

I worked across:

My step by step solution:

01Understanding the brand

Before designing screens, I needed to understand what Aierth actually stood for.

The brand was built around a vision of becoming a leading hub for digital learning while helping close the global technology skills gap.

Its education offering spans areas such as:

Cloud Engineering · UI/UX Design · Software Engineering · AI/ML · Cybersecurity · DevOps · Data Analytics

This meant the visual language couldn't feel tied to one technology discipline.

It needed enough flexibility to represent an entire technology ecosystem.

The brand direction was built around the idea that learning should lead somewhere.

Learn → Practice → Build → Become career-ready → Access opportunity

02Creating the visual direction

The visual identity was designed to balance two seemingly different characteristics:

TECHNOLOGY

Precise, modern, structured, intelligent.

HUMAN PROGRESS

Warm, ambitious, accessible, optimistic.

Rather than relying on the typical “dark futuristic tech startup” aesthetic, I explored a more approachable technology language.

The core brand palette was built around:

Aierth Orange → energy, action, and optimism.

Aierth Dark Azure → trust, stability, and technical credibility

Needed for an education and technology company.

Together, they created a visual contrast that could work across both marketing and product interfaces.

03Designing the brand system

Instead of treating the logo, colors, typography, buttons, cards, imagery, and marketing materials as separate pieces, I approached them as one system.

The goal was consistency without making every touchpoint look identical.

Visual personality + Brand system

Modern
Confident
Human
Ambitious
Accessible
Technology-driven

Posts → campaign banner → website → course page → product interface

04From brand to product

One of the most important parts of the project was translating the brand identity into an actual digital experience.

The website needed to answer a user's questions quickly:

What is Aierth?

What can I learn?

Is this for me?

What will I get from it?

Can I trust this platform?

How do I get started?

That led to a website structure centered around discovery and conversion.

Understand Aierth → Find a learning path → See yourself → Know the outcome → Build confidence → Take the next step

Website architecture

05Designing the homepage

The hero section was treated as the first product decision.

Instead of overwhelming visitors with information, the experience

needed to immediately establish:

what Aierth offers + who it helps + what the visitor should do next.

The visual hierarchy therefore prioritized:

01

A strong statement of value.

02

Supporting context.

03

A clear action.

04

Visual proof of the learning experience.

This created a more intentional path from curiosity to action.

06Course discovery

Aierth offers multiple technology learning paths, which created a discoverability problem.

A visitor shouldn't have to understand the entire Aierth ecosystem before finding the right program.

I therefore approached course discovery around recognition rather than explanation.

Users should be able to quickly identify:

What am I interested in?

What level am I at?

Where can this skill take me?

This informed the use of clear course cards, categorization, concise descriptions, visual hierarchy, and prominent CTAs.

This created a more intentional path from curiosity to action.

07Designing for conversion

The website wasn't designed simply to look impressive.

Every major section had a job.

This transformed the homepage from a collection of sections into a conversion journey.

Hero

(Create immediate understanding)

Program section

(Create exploration)

Benefits

(Create desire)

Testimonials

(Reduce uncertainty)

Career outcomes

(Create motivation)

CTA

(Convert interest into action)

This transformed the homepage from a collection of sections into a conversion journey.

08Designing the enrollment experience

One of the business realities I had to account for was that Aierth's audience includes people at very different stages of their technology journey.

Someone could be:

Completely new to tech

Switching careers

Upskilling

Looking for freelance opportunities

Preparing for a professional role

The experience therefore needed to feel encouraging rather than exclusive.

The language and interface direction focused on:

clarity over complexity

action over jargon

progress over perfection

What they saw after Clicking on “Enroll”

09Marketing became part of the product

Aierth wasn't only a website project.

The brand needed to live wherever prospective students encountered it.

I extended the design thinking into campaign and promotional materials, including cohort campaigns and enrollment messaging.

10Building a flexible design language

A major consideration was scalability.

Aierth wasn't going to remain a single website.

The business could eventually include:

Academy → Courses → Learning platform → Community → Talent marketplace → Career opportunities

That meant the design language had to survive beyond the original website.

I approached components with reuse in mind:

  • Navigation
  • Buttons
  • Course cards
  • Feature cards
  • Testimonials
  • CTA sections
  • Form elements
  • Promotional banners
  • Content sections
  • Responsive layouts

The objective was to create a foundation that could evolve as the product ecosystem grew.

The product thinking behind the visuals

One of the biggest lessons from the project was that visual design alone couldn't solve the experience.

For example:

A beautiful course card doesn't matter if users don't understand what happens after clicking it.

A strong hero doesn't matter if the CTA leads to a confusing flow.

A powerful campaign doesn't matter if the landing experience doesn't deliver on its promise.

So I constantly asked:

What does the user need to know next?

That question became one of the simplest but most useful principles throughout the project.

Designing for trust

Education is a high-trust product.

Users are potentially investing:

money + time + career expectations

So the interface needed to communicate credibility.

I used hierarchy, consistency, social proof, course information, instructor/content context, clear CTAs, and structured layouts to reduce uncertainty.

The current Aierth experience similarly emphasizes practical projects, career support, certifications, student outcomes, and access to global opportunities.

Beyond education

The most interesting part of the Aierth project was realizing that the brand could become bigger than an academy.

Aierth's current ecosystem describes a broader ambition: training African technology talent and eventually connecting that talent with global opportunities through Aeternum Africa.

That made the original design challenge even more relevant.

The brand needed to be capable of growing from:

Education

into:

Education + Talent + Opportunity

This influenced the decision to create a visual language that felt broad enough for future digital products rather than locking the identity into “online course platform.

Designing for trust

Education is a high-trust product.

Users are potentially investing:

money + time + career expectations

So the interface needed to communicate credibility.

I used hierarchy, consistency, social proof, course information, instructor/content context, clear CTAs, and structured layouts to reduce uncertainty.

The current Aierth experience similarly emphasizes practical projects, career support, certifications, student outcomes, and access to global opportunities.

The design principle

Build the bridge.

Aierth sits between two worlds:

Potential ←→ Opportunity

The learner has potential.

The industry has opportunity.

Aierth's product experience exists in the middle.

The brand therefore became less about simply saying:

“Learn technology.”

And more about communicating:

“Develop the skills that can move your life forward.”

Outcome

The result was a brand and digital experience designed to give Aierth a stronger foundation as it moved from an emerging education business toward a broader technology ecosystem.

The work established:

A recognizable visual direction

A consistent digital language

A clearer website structure

A stronger course discovery experience

Conversion-focused page architecture

A reusable UI foundation

A marketing system that could extend beyond the website

Most importantly, the design created a relationship between the brand promise and the product experience.

The brand says:

There is opportunity.

The product says:

Here's how you get there.

From Brand Idea to Intelligent Product

Chimamanda — Aierth’s AI Assistant

As Aierth evolved beyond being a learning platform, I wanted the brand to have a more human and accessible way for users to interact with its digital ecosystem. This led me to propose Chimamanda — Aierth’s AI Assistant to make enrollment easier and faster,and to also evolve as aierth’s market place AI assistant, envisioned as a conversational layer across the platform, similar to how banking products use assistants to make complex services easier to access.

I developed the initial product idea, defined how Chimamanda should fit into the Aierth experience, and designed the interaction model around a simple principle: users should be able to ask for what they need instead of searching through multiple pages to find it.

Rather than creating an AI chatbot simply because AI was trending, I approached Chimamanda as a product feature with specific jobs to perform. The assistant was designed to help prospective students discover suitable programs, answer common questions about Aierth, explain learning pathways, guide users through onboarding, surface relevant platform information, and direct more complex requests to the appropriate support channel.

From a technology training idea to a brand designed for an ecosystem.

Aierth was an opportunity to work at the intersection of brand strategy, product design, business goals, and human ambition.

I wasn't just designing pages.

I was helping define how an emerging technology company could look, communicate, and behave across its digital experience.

And that is what made this project particularly valuable to me as a product designer:

I learned that the strongest product experiences don't just help people use a product.

They help people believe in what the product can make possible.

What I learned

Brand and product shouldn't be separate projects

The visual identity, website, course experience, and marketing materials all communicate the same promise. Designing them together created a more consistent experience.

Education products need emotional design.

People invest money, time, and career expectations in education. Clear learning paths, approachable language, and credible evidence help people feel confident about their next step.

Scalability needs to be designed early.

Reusable navigation, buttons, cards, forms, and responsive patterns gave Aierth a foundation that could grow beyond its first website.

The best interfaces reduce uncertainty.

At every stage, I asked: What does the user need to know next? Clear course information and thoughtful conversion journeys helped connect interest with action.
